title: Black Tie

jokes.text: Yo' mama is so stupid, she thinks an iMac is a new hamburger at McDonald's.
jokes.setup: The writers' room is doing a yo' mama joke battle
jokes.punchline: iMac / McDonald's — the joke works on the Mac prefix but is a fairly standard yo' mama format
jokes.explanation: Functional yo' mama joke with a mildly clever tech/fast-food angle. Sets up the writers' room context but isn't exceptional. The iMac pun is the only real craft here.

jokes.text: What's the difference between yo' mama and a washing machine? When I drop a load in the washing machine, it doesn't follow me around for a week.
jokes.setup: Liz builds a setup that sounds like a standard yo' mama riddle format
jokes.punchline: The punchline is shockingly crude and sexual coming from Liz, subverting her straight-laced persona
jokes.explanation: The joke lands because it comes from Liz Lemon — the audience doesn't expect her to win the yo' mama battle this emphatically or this crudely. Strong structure (classic riddle form), economical, and the character incongruity gives it extra punch. Not quite landmark material but clearly the best joke so far.

jokes.text: Lemon, could I speak with you alone for a moment? / That's what your sister asked me last night. Booyah!
jokes.setup: Jack interrupts the yo' mama battle with a professional request
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately fires back with a 'your sister' yo' mama-style burn directed at Jack, completely out of character for their dynamic
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is Liz refusing to drop the joke-battle mode even when her boss walks in. The 'booyah' seals it. It's a strong character beat — Liz being socially inappropriate — and the timing works well as an escalation of the yo' mama sequence.

jokes.text: Jack asks what Liz knows about the Hapsburg empire and she says she studied 'Theatre tech'
jokes.setup: Jack references the Austro-Hungarian Empire and the Defenestration of Prague, expecting Liz to follow
jokes.punchline: Liz says she studied 'Theatre tech' in college, as if that explains everything
jokes.explanation: Classic 30 Rock character comedy: Jack's erudite world-weariness runs smack into Liz's unpretentious mediocrity. 'Theatre tech' is the perfect answer — not even 'theatre,' but the backstage technical side. Jack's 'I see' sells it perfectly.

jokes.text: Would I have to wear high-heel shoes? / Yes. / This will be good for you.
jokes.setup: Jack is inviting Liz to a glamorous social event
jokes.punchline: Liz's main concern is whether she has to wear heels — a deeply un-glamorous objection that deflates the grandiosity of the invitation
jokes.explanation: Pure Liz Lemon character comedy. The heel concern is exactly the wrong priority for this moment, which is what makes it funny. Economical and character-specific.

jokes.text: You're even wearing lipstick. / No. They're just really chapped.
jokes.setup: Jack is encouraging Liz, noting she looks better than usual — 'you're even wearing lipstick'
jokes.punchline: Liz denies the compliment entirely with a medical explanation: her lips are chapped
jokes.explanation: Concise and perfectly calibrated. The joke is maximally economical: one line that simultaneously characterizes Liz (perpetually unglamorous, physically neglected) and deflates Jack's attempt at a compliment. 'They're just really chapped' is a great line — specific, pitiable, and funny.

jokes.text: That's what your mom said to me last night. Booyah. / You got slammed, girl. That was surprising.
jokes.setup: Liz and Jack wrap up their conversation; Jenna witnesses
jokes.punchline: Liz does another yo' mama callback on Jack; Jenna's 'that was surprising' is the button — acknowledging even she didn't expect it
jokes.explanation: The callback works and Jenna's meta-commentary ('that was surprising') adds a nice layer. Slightly diminishing returns compared to the first 'booyah' moment, but still lands because of the running gag structure.

jokes.text: Pete doing an Elmo voice on the phone: 'Elmo wants you to aim your pee-pee at the potty. No, not at Mommy. At the potty.'
jokes.setup: Pete is on the phone, doing potty training with his child via his wife, using an Elmo voice
jokes.punchline: The child has apparently aimed at Mommy instead of the potty — revealed through Pete's mortified correction
jokes.explanation: The gag layers well: Pete doing the Elmo voice publicly is embarrassing enough, but the implied pee-on-Mommy disaster escalates it perfectly. The economy of inference — we only hear Pete's side — is well executed.

jokes.text: How is that Elmo's fault? / Did Mommy have some wine before she called Elmo?
jokes.setup: The potty-training disaster is apparently being blamed on Pete/Elmo by his wife on the phone
jokes.punchline: Pete fires back in Elmo-voice suggesting his wife has been drinking — a shocking implication delivered in a children's character voice
jokes.explanation: The comedy of a man asking his wife if she's been drinking while maintaining an Elmo voice is inspired. The contrast between the children's register and the adult accusation is sharp. Strong economy and originality.

jokes.text: Pete, there are two types of women in this world — one who gives you strength and one who takes strength from you, like Delilah took strength from Samson in that movie.
jokes.setup: Tracy is giving Pete advice about his wife
jokes.punchline: 'In that movie' — Tracy thinks the Biblical story of Samson and Delilah is a movie, which is both ignorant and perfectly in character
jokes.explanation: Tracy's malapropism of the Bible as 'that movie' is perfectly character-specific — his cultural illiteracy is so consistent it feels earned. The setup sounds like genuine wisdom before the punchline undermines it. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: I actually haven't met your wife yet. Hi. / That ain't my wife. Go get me a fizzy water.
jokes.setup: Tracy tells Pete he loves his wife and she makes him feel like a man; a woman is nearby whom Pete hasn't met
jokes.punchline: Pete greets the woman assuming she's Tracy's wife; Tracy dismisses her as some random woman and immediately commands her to fetch him a drink
jokes.explanation: Perfectly timed and economical. The joke is Tracy's total casualness — he's been extolling his wife's virtues while a random woman stands nearby, and he redirects her instantly with no embarrassment. 'Go get me a fizzy water' is a great button.

jokes.text: Samson! / Great shoving, Mr. Jordan.
jokes.setup: Tracy wraps up his Samson philosophy speech
jokes.punchline: Tracy apparently shoves someone while yelling 'Samson!' — someone compliments him on his 'great shoving,' implying this is a known Tracy behavior
jokes.explanation: The 'great shoving' compliment implies this is routine — people around Tracy are trained to encourage his random physical outbursts. The visual of Tracy shoving someone mid-monologue and receiving professional praise for it is absurdly funny. Rewatch bonus because you catch 'great shoving' more on repeat.

jokes.text: What's that for? / I'm going to a birthday party for some prince tonight. / You mean like a dog birthday party?
jokes.setup: Liz is dressed up for the Hapsburg birthday party; Jenna sees the fancy outfit
jokes.punchline: Jenna's first assumption is that 'prince' means a dog named Prince — a reveal of either profound stupidity or eccentric worldview
jokes.explanation: Quick, sharp, and character-specific. Jenna's obliviousness is endearing rather than cruel. The dog birthday party assumption is a great misdirect — it's not the obvious wrong answer, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Jack presents Liz with the dress — Liz goes to shake his hand, hurts herself on the box, reacts with 'Ow! That really hurt my hand! Dag! Who does that?!'
jokes.setup: Jack presents Liz with a gift box — in a romantic-gesture context from a sophisticated man, the expected response is gracious acceptance
jokes.punchline: Liz apparently tries to shake the box or handle it awkwardly and hurts herself, reacting with completely unglamorous outrage ('Dag! Who does that?!')
jokes.explanation: Classic Liz Lemon: she can't even receive a gift gracefully. 'Dag! Who does that?!' is perfectly unglamorous. Physical comedy inferred from the transcript, rewatch bonus for seeing the actual gesture.

jokes.text: Jenna insists 'This is definitely a date.' Liz says 'No.' Jenna: 'Is it?'
jokes.setup: Liz insists the party isn't a date with Jack
jokes.punchline: Jenna's 'Is it?' is a playful non-argument — she's not convinced but also not sure
jokes.explanation: A light comedic beat that plants the 'is it a date' running gag. The 'Is it?' is charming but not a standout line.

jokes.text: At the party, Liz asks if it's a date; Jack laughs dismissively: 'Lemon, I date socialites and models and actresses, Liz Hurley... in the '90s.'
jokes.setup: Liz wonders if this is a date; Jack goes to reassure her
jokes.punchline: He names Liz Hurley but qualifies it with 'in the '90s' — implying she's no longer at that level, or that even his conquests are dated
jokes.explanation: The '...in the '90s' qualifier does a lot of work — it signals Jack's elitism while also quietly self-deprecating. The list 'socialites, models, actresses' builds perfectly to the specific and slightly deflated Hurley reference.

jokes.text: Oh, Liz, if you dress well and enter with confidence, you can get in anywhere. / You showed the security guy your boobs, didn't you? / Just one. It's not the White House.
jokes.setup: Jenna appears at the exclusive party uninvited; she claims confidence and good dress are sufficient to enter anywhere
jokes.punchline: Liz calls her bluff; Jenna confirms she flashed the guard but calibrates: 'Just one. It's not the White House.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The setup creates a false premise (confidence = access), Liz correctly decodes it, and Jenna's confirmation is perfect — but it's 'Just one. It's not the White House.' that makes this exceptional. That line implies: (a) she has a calibrated protocol for this, (b) she HAS done it at the White House (requiring both), and (c) she considers this perfectly reasonable. Maximum information per word, specific, quotable, and completely character-specific to Jenna. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor example in craft and economy.

jokes.text: When I'm the queen of Australia, I'll have him executed. / Austria. / Yeah. That's what I said.
jokes.setup: Jenna is fantasizing about marrying Gerhardt; Liz corrects her geography
jokes.punchline: Jenna doubles down — 'Yeah. That's what I said' — not realizing the difference between Australia and Austria
jokes.explanation: The Australia/Austria confusion is a classic but the 'That's what I said' button — her confidence in her own wrongness — elevates it above a simple malapropism. Jenna's obliviousness is perfectly rendered.

jokes.text: Prince Gerhardt enters — visibly severely inbred, with physical deformities suggesting centuries of Hapsburg inbreeding. 'Wow. Who's Snow White now?'
jokes.setup: Jenna called Liz Snow White and said she'd 'party with the little people'; Gerhardt's condition has been described as requiring him to 'stave off infection'
jokes.punchline: Gerhardt's dramatic entrance reveals he is extremely short/physically unusual due to inbreeding — Liz turns the Snow White insult back on Jenna
jokes.explanation: The callback to the Snow White insult is perfectly timed and structurally satisfying — the show set up the punchline three minutes earlier. Gerhardt's visual reveal IS the joke, and Liz's callback line is the perfect button. Strong structure and rewatch bonus for catching the full setup-payoff arc.

jokes.text: Cut to Gerhardt at 7:45: '7:45, and I'm still awake. [Laughing]'
jokes.setup: Gerhardt appears to be enjoying the party
jokes.punchline: He celebrates being awake at 7:45 — implying his health is so precarious that surviving to early evening is an achievement
jokes.explanation: Short, dark, and devastating. Gerhardt laughing with genuine joy at being awake at 7:45 PM is a perfect comedic distillation of his character — the inbred Habsburg who shouldn't still be alive. Maximum economy: five words, huge implication.

jokes.text: And how did you two meet? / It was part of the Big Brother Little Sister program.
jokes.setup: Bianca asks how Jack and Liz know each other — expecting a romantic origin story given the context of the party
jokes.punchline: Jack claims it's the Big Brother/Little Sister program — implying he's Liz's older male mentor, which is simultaneously a put-down and a plausible description of their relationship
jokes.explanation: Sharp and multi-layered: it's an insult to Liz (she's his charity case), a cover story, and an accurate description of their dynamic all at once. The 'Little' in Little Sister stings extra. Very economical.

jokes.text: His highness has noticed you. / His highness is attempting to wink at you. / [Beat — Gerhardt's wink is clearly not working as intended]
jokes.setup: Gerhardt has sent his aide to invite Liz to dine next to him — a formal, courtly gesture
jokes.punchline: The aide reports that Gerhardt is 'attempting to wink' — the verb 'attempting' implies his physical condition makes even winking a challenge requiring narration
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely in the word 'attempting.' The formality of the aide narrating Gerhardt's physical struggle as if announcing a royal decree is inspired. It also works as a visual gag — the audience sees whatever horrifying wink Gerhardt produces. 'Attempting to wink' is one of the episode's most quotable lines and comparable to the 8.0 anchor in economy and originality.

jokes.text: Who knows how long this show will last. And I have no other skills whatsoever.
jokes.setup: Jenna is rationalizing pursuing Gerhardt — she needs someone to take care of her, she's not going to be gorgeous forever
jokes.punchline: She drops in 'Who knows how long this show will last' — a meta-reference to the show's actual precarious status as a new series, then confirms she has no other skills
jokes.explanation: The meta-reference is well-integrated into Jenna's character logic (she's genuinely worried about her career) rather than being a cheap wink at the audience. Rewatch bonus because knowing the show survived makes this ironic.

jokes.text: Liz says she doesn't think Gerhardt can 'take care' of Jenna; Jenna: 'And I can get past someone's looks.' Liz: 'Since when?' Jenna: 'I'm an actress, Liz. It would be my greatest role of all time.'
jokes.setup: Jenna claims she can look past Gerhardt's appearance
jokes.punchline: 'I'm an actress, Liz. It would be my greatest role of all time.' — framing pretending to love someone as an acting challenge
jokes.explanation: Excellent Jenna character comedy. The logic is perfect — she's so dedicated to acting that she frames a cynical marriage as her Meryl Streep moment. 'My greatest role of all time' is a great button.

jokes.text: Pete suddenly acting dominant with the strip club woman — 'Mind your business, son!' / He's embracing his power. / [Growls]
jokes.setup: Pete has been emasculated all episode (Elmo phone call, submissive marriage); Tracy's Samson speech seems to be having an effect
jokes.punchline: Pete snaps into alpha mode — growls, tells someone to mind their business — and Tracy narrates it approvingly: 'He's embracing his power'
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Pete's emasculation arc. Tracy's role as life coach is funny in itself, and 'He's embracing his power' as narration is good. The growl is a nice physical button.

jokes.text: So now I keep it simple. Nothing but endless, meaningless one-night stands with a carousel of super-hot women I couldn't care less about. / That's heartbreaking.
jokes.setup: Jack explains how he's coped since Bianca left him
jokes.punchline: 'Endless, meaningless one-night stands with a carousel of super-hot women I couldn't care less about' is framed as the tragic downgrade; Liz's 'That's heartbreaking' plays it completely straight
jokes.explanation: The joke is the inversion: Jack is genuinely sad that his life consists of sleeping with supermodels. Liz playing it completely straight ('That's heartbreaking') is perfect — she accepts the premise without irony. 'Carousel of super-hot women' is a great phrase. Strong character integration for both.

jokes.text: But I would enjoy watching you dance for me.
jokes.setup: Having declined to dance, Gerhardt still wants engagement
jokes.punchline: He requests a private performance with an oddly formal, entitled register — 'I would enjoy watching you dance for me' is both courtly and slightly ominous
jokes.explanation: The formal register ('I would enjoy') applied to a personal entertainment request is perfectly Gerhardt. It's the tone of a man accustomed to being obeyed. Builds perfectly from the joint fluid line.

jokes.text: Jazz! / Tap! / Jitterbug! / Charleston! / Interpretive! / Twirl! / Twirl again! / Keep twirling!
jokes.setup: Jenna is dancing for Gerhardt; he is calling out dance styles
jokes.punchline: The escalation from legitimate dance forms (Jazz, Tap, Jitterbug) to commands ('Twirl! Twirl again! Keep twirling!') reveals the regal entitlement degenerating into pure personal amusement
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is masterful: starting with recognizable dance forms gives it credibility, then 'Interpretive!' signals the shift, then pure repetitive commands ('Twirl! Twirl again! Keep twirling!') reveal that Gerhardt is just a powerful man entertaining himself. The repetition of 'Twirl' is the joke — the joke gets bigger the more he repeats it. Strong rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: Everyone thinks I'm 5'5", but I'm only 5'4". / Wow! That is an amazing story!
jokes.setup: Pete is apparently talking to the woman, who is engaged
jokes.punchline: Pete's 'amazing story' is that he is one inch shorter than people think — delivered as a confidence with weight; the woman's enthusiastic response ('Wow! That is an amazing story!') suggests Pete has charmed her with literally nothing
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The comedy operates on multiple levels: (1) the 'secret' is utterly mundane (1 inch height discrepancy), (2) Pete delivers it as if it's a genuine confession, (3) the woman finds it 'amazing' — suggesting either she is genuinely easy to impress or Pete has somehow found the exact thing that works on this particular person. The response mirrors the joke — Pete's non-story told as a story, validated as an amazing story. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in originality and structure.

jokes.text: Kenneth showing up to warn Pete: 'Do you remember the movie Footloose, where those evil kids won in the end? / You're going to make a mistake tonight. You gonna make a mistake tonight!'
jokes.setup: Kenneth has arrived to warn Pete about making a mistake with the woman
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's version of Footloose has the evil kids winning — a completely wrong reading of the film that reveals Kenneth's genuinely peculiar moral worldview
jokes.explanation: Brilliant character joke. Kenneth's version of Footloose — where 'those evil kids won in the end' — is either a profound misreading of the film or a window into Kenneth's deeply conservative worldview where the dancing teenagers ARE the evil ones. The ambiguity is what makes it genius. This could only be Kenneth. Strong character integration and originality — one of the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: Lick her face. Think of God.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is delivering anti-temptation advice
jokes.punchline: 'Lick her face' as a deterrence strategy — an utterly inexplicable tactic that only makes sense as a way to break the romantic spell through deliberate awkwardness
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Lick her face. Think of God.' is perfectly Kenneth — his advice is simultaneously well-intentioned, bizarre, and completely without self-awareness. The pairing ('Lick her face' + 'Think of God') is inspired: two entirely different types of deterrence presented as equally valid. Maximum economy (four words, two strategies). Highly quotable and deeply character-specific. Near the top of the episode's best moments.

jokes.text: I know. I just wanted to talk to you. / Oh, no. You don't need to do that. [Banging on door] / I've never done it in a men's bathroom before. / Well, in this building.
jokes.setup: Vikki has followed Pete into the men's bathroom, claiming she just wants to talk
jokes.punchline: 'I've never done it in a men's bathroom before.' / 'Well, in this building.' — she's been with him elsewhere in the building but not specifically in this building's men's room
jokes.explanation: The 'well, in this building' qualifier is the joke — she's not denying promiscuity, just adding geographical precision. The specificity ('in this building') is what elevates it from a standard sex joke to something with real craft. It implies an entire history in other buildings' bathrooms. Strong economy and structure.

jokes.text: Bianca corners Liz: 'Are you going to marry Jack?' Liz: 'Uh, I don't know. We've talked about it.' [Pause] 'I can tell from the way he looks at you that he's serious. He's going to get you pregnant right away. I'm sure. A little late-in-life baby he can parade around Nantucket.'
jokes.setup: Bianca confronts the 'fake girlfriend' Liz about her relationship with Jack
jokes.punchline: Bianca lays out an oddly specific and bitterly detailed prediction — 'a little late-in-life baby he can parade around Nantucket' — revealing her deep jealousy and knowledge of Jack
jokes.explanation: 'A little late-in-life baby he can parade around Nantucket' is extremely specific and very funny. The Nantucket detail is perfect — it's not just a baby, it's a status accessory for the Nantucket set. Strong character work for Bianca.

jokes.text: He's going to get you pregnant right away. I'm sure. A little late-in-life baby he can parade around Nantucket.
jokes.setup: Bianca is 'advising' Liz about Jack's patterns
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'parade around Nantucket' — Bianca has clearly seen this playbook before, and she resents the Nantucket baby-parading ritual specifically
jokes.explanation: 'Parade around Nantucket' is specific and rich — it instantly evokes Jack's social world and the performative nature of his relationships. Good character work establishing Bianca's perspective.

jokes.text: I hate seeing Johnny happy!
jokes.setup: Following 'sit on a knife,' Bianca has had a moment to compose herself — or hasn't
jokes.punchline: She simply states her core feeling: 'I hate seeing Johnny happy!' — direct, raw, and perfectly villainous while also being oddly relatable
jokes.explanation: The distilled version of everything Bianca feels. 'I hate seeing Johnny happy' is both a perfect villain line and a weirdly honest confession. Maximum economy — six words that define the character. The callback to the previous emotional admission gives this button extra resonance.

jokes.text: Jenna, I know we have just met, but I think I love you. / Do you love me? / Mm... hmm.
jokes.setup: Gerhardt has fallen for Jenna after her dance performance
jokes.punchline: Jenna's 'Mm... hmm' — a beat of consideration before committing to a declaration of love to a severely inbred prince she just met
jokes.explanation: Jenna's deliberative 'Mm... hmm' does comedy work — she's actually weighing it — but the joke is more about the situation than any specific line. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Knowing that I have the love of a beautiful woman has set me free!
jokes.setup: Gerhardt receives Jenna's declaration of love
jokes.punchline: His euphoric declaration 'has set me free!' — delivered at maximum dramatic register — is immediately followed by physical consequences
jokes.explanation: The dramatic declaration that immediately precedes physical collapse is a classic escalation setup. Works well in context as part of Gerhardt's arc.

jokes.text: Who let him drink champagne? He cannot metabolize the grapes!
jokes.setup: Gerhardt appears to be dying or collapsing after drinking champagne
jokes.punchline: 'He cannot metabolize the grapes!' — the aide's panicked diagnosis reveals that grapes are another thing Gerhardt's severely compromised body cannot process
jokes.explanation: Exceptional. 'He cannot metabolize the grapes!' is a line that sounds like it should be a normal medical emergency statement but is profoundly absurd — grapes, not alcohol, not sulfites, but THE GRAPES. The specificity is what makes it legendary. The panic register is perfect. One of the episode's most quotable lines.

jokes.text: Someone call Dr. Spaceman!
jokes.setup: Medical emergency — Gerhardt is collapsing
jokes.punchline: Dr. Spaceman (pronounced Spa-CHEM-an) is apparently the go-to doctor at the party — an inherently absurd name for a medical professional, suggesting the worst possible medical care is on its way
jokes.explanation: Dr. Spaceman is a recurring 30 Rock character, so this functions as a running gag callback for regular viewers. The name alone is funny, but the panic context makes it funnier — this is who they're calling in a medical crisis.

jokes.text: Liz: 'I think she pulled out a chunk of my hair.' Jack: 'Really? Where?' Liz shows him. Jack whistles.
jokes.setup: Liz is assessing damage from the catfight
jokes.punchline: Jack's whistle implies the hair loss is impressively large — a physical understatement through a non-verbal reaction
jokes.explanation: A solid visual reaction beat. The whistle is a concise way to convey the scale of damage, and it's character-appropriate for Jack to be mildly impressed rather than concerned.

jokes.text: Meine Damen und Herren! The Hapsburg line... has ended. / You can pick up your gift bags at the coat check.
jokes.setup: Gerhardt appears to have died; the aide makes the announcement
jokes.punchline: The announcement of the end of the Hapsburg dynasty — centuries of European history — is immediately followed by the most mundane party logistics: gift bag pickup
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. The structure is flawless: grand announcement of the extinction of a royal bloodline ('The Hapsburg line... has ended') — possibly the most historically momentous thing anyone could say — followed immediately by 'You can pick up your gift bags at the coat check.' The juxtaposition of world-historical significance and party logistics is perfect. The pause between 'has ended' and the coat check announcement is the structure working at maximum efficiency. This is the kind of joke that defines the show's sensibility. Highest scores in the episode.

jokes.text: Oh, just to know that she's filled with bile over me warms my heart.
jokes.setup: Jack continues processing his emotional satisfaction
jokes.punchline: The inversion: knowing his ex is miserable 'warms his heart' — a phrase usually reserved for positive feelings, here applied to someone else's misery
jokes.explanation: Classic ironic inversion — 'warms my heart' applied to bile. Solid but not exceptional; the more memorable version of this sentiment was already expressed by Bianca herself ('I hate seeing Johnny happy').

jokes.text: I had 'lunch' with Martha Stewart and 'dinner' with her daughter, Alexis.
jokes.setup: Jack is continuing his list of conquests to disabuse Liz of any romantic notions
jokes.punchline: The air quotes around 'lunch' and 'dinner' imply sexual encounters. Then: he had 'lunch' (sex) with Martha Stewart AND 'dinner' (sex) with her daughter Alexis — implying he slept with both mother and daughter, in that order, the same day
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best jokes and an extremely strong way to end the episode. The air quotes do all the structural work — the audience gets 'lunch' and prepares for the same joke with 'dinner,' but the reveal that it's ALSO the daughter makes it exponentially darker. The real-name specificity (Martha Stewart, Alexis) makes it both funnier and more audacious. 'Gross.' from Liz is the perfect one-word button. Extremely quotable, dark, and structurally precise. Third-best joke of the episode.

tmdb_overview: Liz wonders if she's actually on a date with Jack as she accompanies him to a birthday celebration for a foreign prince. While at the ball, Liz sees a different side to Jack as he unexpectedly runs in to his ex-wife. Back at 30 Rock, Tracy tempts Pete with a booze- and babe-filled party in the office, while Kenneth tries to keep Pete on the straight and narrow.
insight: Fifty-five jokes in 19 minutes—rapid-fire character comedy sustains a solid B+ episode.
